Pedro Almodóvar Didn’t Think He Could Write a Novel. But Once He Started, the “Story Began to Pour Out”

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall.
  • In a recent development, this brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes.
  • Recent findings suggest that both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall. For now, I’ll accept that it is Cruz because the image is on a poster for Broken Embraces, a 2009 film she starred in. My hesitation in believing it’s her, however, is because finding a resemblance between the woman on the poster and Cruz requires a lot of generosity. It’s as if the artist had painted her based on a detailed description he’d heard, but he’d never actually seen his subject onscreen. “We were given this in India,” explains Pedro Almodóvar’s brother, Agustín, the head and owner of El Deseo, the production manufacturer behind Almodóvar’s films. “Specialized artists still hand-paint their movie posters, and the results are images like this.” The work’s imperfections give it a charm that no poster created by AI could ever match.

In a recent development, this brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. It depicts a Blade Runner–style dystopian future where replicants, jaded by digital perfection, are fascinated by the rough edges of human culture. The book has just been published in Spain (it is scheduled to be published in the United States, in Spanish, in February 2027), following the release of Almodóvar’s latest film, Bitter Christmas (which will be in select US theaters on November 13, and released nationwide on November 25).

Recent findings suggest that both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator. At the same time, they are clearly different from Almodóvar, like the difference between Cruz and the woman on the Indian movie poster.

Sources indicate that I ask Almodóvar why he decided to recount Flavio’s story in the form of a novel rather than a movie, but he appears to have not heard my question and answers instead as if I’d asked him why it took him so long to publish a novel, which is undoubtedly much more interesting: “I think the reason I hadn’t written a novel until now was that I wasn’t sure I’d be able to, even though I’d wanted to write one since I was a young man. At first, however, I didn’t even know myself that this story would be a novel. I started with a simple anecdote about an acting coach and an actor, and that opened the floodgates; the story began to pour out. When it was already over 30 pages, I sent it to my editor. He told me there was a novel there and that I should keep going.”.

The 77-year-old director from La Mancha poses in a jacket, polo shirt, pants, and sneakers by Loewe.

It has been revealed that he will answer many other questions that I haven’t asked but should have: “I didn’t know, for example, that I’d include my story ‘Addiction,’ which is a little treat for fans that had already appeared in Pain and Glory. It was going to be a monologue that Carmen Machi would perform in a small theater, but I ended up giving it to Asier Etxeandia in that film. I also wrote Pain and Glory very promptly. And in it, I inserted, like little snippets, more pieces that I’d already written. For example, there’s another story, just five pages long, about a chance encounter with an actor with whom I’d had a very bad relationship in the past [Eusebio Poncela, who starred in Law of Desire 40 years ago] and with whom, in the story, I ended up doing heroin. In real life, the fact that he was using heroin while we were filming was the reason we had a falling out. Thanks to those preexisting elements, which fit into the story, I was able to write that movie so quickly. And the same is true of my upcoming book. What defines it is a sense of absolute freedom.”.

And maybe that sentence is, in the end, the answer to all my questions for Almodóvar.

Vanity Fair España: Is that sense of freedom why you decided to write a novel instead of a screenplay?

Pedro Almodóvar: In Bitter Christmas, Leonardo Sbaraglia’s character claims he needs absolute freedom to work. Just like me throughout my entire career. That freedom feels more intense with a novel because it’s a format with which I have less experience. I’ve woven it together from different stories, but they all revolve around the protagonist and it’s been very satisfying. It wasn’t a whim: The book has the same rigor to it as everything else I do, but that freedom is deeply rooted in my style. That’s why I wrote it so quickly. Everything flowed naturally.

It has been revealed that there is a tradition of using a novel as a container for many stories, as with Don Quixote or Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa. On the other hand, speaking of influences, it’s interesting that when you wrote your Patty Diphusa stories in 1983 [included in Patty Diphusa and Other Writings, published by Faber & Faber in 1992], Anita Loos and pornographic photo novels are influences that appear in the mix, but in The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes, you turn to, let’s say, more distinguished names: Henry James, Nabokov, and Colm Tóibín, who even appears as a character.

I’m not trying to compare myself to Cervantes or Potocki, but yes, that’s what the book is. That’s precisely why this novel can’t be adapted for the screen: You’d have to choose one part of it and develop it, but as it stands now, that wouldn’t be possible. Those earlier influences are still with me—Anita Loos is certainly among them—and they continue to inspire me with both specific phrases and broader themes. In the novel, I name authors who inspire me and with whom I connect organically, such as Joan Didion and Virginia Woolf. But Patty and Flavio have something in common: a sense of urgency that drives them to write at a breakneck pace, out of a physiological need. Neither of them sleeps much, though in Patty’s case it’s because she can’t stop doing cocaine. Beyond that, other differences set them apart, including the differences between what life was like in the ’80s and what it’s like now.

What sort of differences are there, and where are they most apparent?

Recent findings suggest that take sex, for example. Patty Diphusa is an archetype of the 1980s, a time of absolute freedom in Spain, and her character can only be understood in the context of the utterly carefree and hedonistic lifestyle we led back then. If she sucks a guy's dick in a bathroom, she’ll then record her wild thoughts because she considers herself a sort of philosopher of eroticism. Although Flavio is a very free-spirited person, just like the book itself, he belongs to another era and another generation. Here, sex is part of a love story, and his attitude toward it is very different. I devote less space to the erotic scenes in this book because I assume people already know what it’s like to sleep with someone.

Almodóvar, in another room at El Deseo’s headquarters, wearing a Louis Vuitton jacket and a Prada knit polo shirt.

You’ve argued on different occasions that in the 1980s, many people in Spain chose that hedonistic and seemingly frivolous lifestyle as a reaction to the previous era, and that this was a political statement. Now we see a fresh generation adopting a different kind of stance. For example, all across Europe, people are taking to the streets to demand their right to housing and decent living conditions, and there’s not much frivolity in that. How do you interpret this change?

Recent findings suggest that I completely empathize with and support the people filling the streets. They are demanding fundamental rights that are enshrined in the Spanish constitution and which are now in jeopardy: housing, health care, and education. I went to the encampment on the Puerta del Sol [in Madrid] only a few times, because I was in Fresh York presenting Bitter Christmas at the New York Film Festival and also because I think a famous person doesn’t really fit in at these demonstrations—if we go, we distort the spirit of it. But I did go, and I bought them food because that’s what I thought they’d need, even though they told me they’d be better off with some tables. I don’t just support their initiative; I’m glad it happened. One thing I’d heard about young people, a generation I don’t know much about, was from a news article that mentioned that 25% of young Spaniards wouldn’t mind living under a dictatorship like Franco’s. I shuddered. What happened in the Puerta del Sol demonstrates that there’s a whole crowd of young people beyond those who go to Ferraz to pray the rosary [since November 2023, a group of Catholic protesters has gathered daily to pray outside the headquarters of the PSOE, Spain’s socialist party, on Madrid’s Calle Ferraz]. They aren’t rich, and they don’t have their lives figured out; they can’t work in the professions they studied to pursue, and they don’t earn enough money to buy homes. That’s terrifying. And the political parties have shown their true colors when it comes to housing. Of course, the PSOE is late to the game with the so-called Maricarmen decrees [a series of measures named after Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her home and subsequent death in October galvanized activists], but at least it has reacted. The starkly different reactions from the Partido Popular [Popular Party] and Vox [center-right and far-right parties, respectively] already tell you what they think about this issue.

Would you agree today with that line from Gloria Muñoz in The Flower of My Secret: “With so much reality, the country’s ready to explode”?

She was talking in literary terms, but it’s true that this phrase has taken on a life of its own over time and has spilled over into other areas. The same thing has happened to another phrase: “A woman is more authentic the more she resembles the person she has dreamed of becoming,” as Agrado mentioned in All About My Mother. It was a line written for a transgender woman, and one that makes perfect sense for her. But now it can be understood in relation to any kind of character: It speaks to authenticity, to staying true to oneself and to one’s own dreams. In the case of young people in our country, we’re talking about a social reality. The country has changed a lot, and we’re very polarized—though France is even worse off than Spain. Europe is in very bad shape overall. The kind of news coverage being produced plays a major role in this rise of the far right. Since the images promoted by the right are so jarring and sensationalist, TV stations pick up on them, and in doing so, they’re effectively promoting figures like Vito Quiles [a far-right activist and influencer]. Damn it, don’t put Vito Quiles on TV—it’s better if we don’t even know where he is or what he’s doing!

Are you particularly concerned about the attention that the far right is getting?

People like [Santiago] Abascal [president of the Vox political party] and [Javier]Milei [president of Argentina] want to do away with the state. Milei, the biggest loudmouth of them all, even aims to destroy the state from within the state itself, which is diabolical. I cite Milei as an example because he says so himself. And on top of that, people elect him for that very reason: He’s someone who has come to power democratically, just like [Donald] Trump. So we’re putting the tools of democracy in the hands of someone whose main goal is to destroy it. Furthermore, in a world so polarized—and with a far right that has no qualms about calling itself fascist—the emergence of AI creates a perfect storm.

One of the stories in your book is, in fact, a dystopian tale inspired by Blade Runner, in which large corporations with shadowy agendas seek to create a less human world. You have contributed so much to human creativity. Are you concerned about how that creativity is being taken over by AI?

In a recent development, I’m always open to change. It’s necessary for society to move forward. But I think the encroachment of AI on human agency is terrible. They should start regulating it now. I’m concerned about the jobs it will replace and also the synthetic culture it will create. In fact, a synthetic culture based on data already exists, and it lacks a soul. The genesis of a screenplay must be human, because AI doesn’t have the sense of doubt, the patience, or the capacity for stories to build up layers of meaning, as in Talk to Her and Bad Education. We need a society that cares about culture, promotes it, and supports it, and not a soulless culture focused only on the immediate. I haven’t used AI creatively, nor do I really know how to. But I’m concerned that we’re now unable to tell whether an image is real or not, given the level of perfection this technology has reached. And moreover, behind it all are very powerful people who know no limits.

Sources indicate that on another topic, standards of beauty have changed, with cosmetic surgery and fillers now widely prevalent. For someone who places such importance on the expressions of actors that must also be a cause for concern.

Well, I wouldn’t mind if an actor in one of my movies had had plastic surgery. For example, I wouldn’t turn down Nicole Kidman for that reason—she’s not only a great actor, but she has also had plastic surgery, and she looks better than ever. Because, these days, actors who’ve had plastic surgery are part of the landscape. It’s so common that you no longer have to explain that a character has had it done; it’s accepted as a matter of course. What’s more, cosmetic surgery has advanced so much that high-profile figures who’ve had work done—like Donatella Versace, Lindsay Lohan, or Nicole Kidman herself—have completely erased the signs of their previous procedures with splendid results. [Editor’s note: Lindsay Lohan has denied having a facelift, while Kidman has never confirmed undergoing any plastic surgery.] The major problem is that, if you make films set in the past, you can’t cast women with plastic surgery or lip fillers; it would be anachronistic, just like putting a piece of furniture from the 1980s in a film about the Spanish Civil War. But it’s true that in my films, plastic surgery hasn’t usually been an option, for aesthetic reasons. Fortunately, there will always be people like Frances McDormand and Carmen Maura. We need older women who look their age.

What interests me most about your new novel is the protagonist’s relationship with an actor, Alez Mazado—a sex symbol who isn’t very intelligent but has a certain natural talent and is open to being molded. Flavio is his Pygmalion. There’s even an explicit reference to Hitchcock’s film Vertigo, which also features that kind of relationship. Do you often have that kind of dynamic with your actors?

I’m like Jimmy Stewart in Vertigo: With actors, I get involved in their hair, lip color, outfits—everything. When I watched Vertigo for the umpteenth time, I thought that character was a director: “He knows exactly what he wants,” they tell him when he takes Kim Novak to try on outfits at a store. The actors I work with and I have adapted to each other, just like in a marriage—in my films, they speak differently; the actors themselves say so. Aitana Sánchez-Gijón told me that she felt she could do anything after playing her role in Bitter Christmas. But I work differently with each actor. With Penélope, for example, I rehearse a lot, and the more we rehearse, the better she gets; then I shoot many takes, and the 10th one is better than the third. And if I can shoot 12, even better. But others don’t like to rehearse, like Antonio Banderas, because he’s a different kind of actor. He has extraordinary intuition and instinct. I don’t need to talk to him as much or push him so hard.

People talk about Los Javis [the moniker for actors turned directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo] as your natural heirs, in the wake of the success of La Bola Negra, which you coproduced through El Deseo. Do you think they will continue your creative legacy?

In a recent development, they definitely treat me like their mentor. They know entire films of mine by heart, even lines that I don’t remember. They’ve been deeply influenced by my films, just as I’ve been influenced by [Luis García] Berlanga, [Rafael] Azcona, [Luis] Buñuel, and [Carlos] Saura. Even if you don’t want to admit it, everyone has role models. I find it flattering, but to say they’re my heirs is to minimize their work. They have a style all their own. In fact, if I were to write the screenplay for La Bola Negra, it would be very different. I don’t feel like their father. I take responsibility for my films and nothing else.

How do you view their film’s unstoppable run at the awards and at the box office?

Los Javis are the major thing right now. Their film is going to be the highest-grossing Spanish movie of all time, although I don’t remember how much The Last Torch Song (1957), starring Sara Montiel, made back in the day. At El Deseo, we’ve had two fantastic years—first with Oliver Laxe’s film [Sirāt], which we also coproduced, and now this one. And I hope the Javis can keep on going and make it through the rest of their promotional tour and then the awards season. From my experience as an Oscar nominee, I know the best moment isn’t when they call your name, but when the ceremony ends. That’s when your life is your own again—whether to start on the next project or simply sleep if that’s what you prefer.

Have you shared that experience with the Javis? Do you give them advice?

Recent findings suggest that just yesterday I texted Javier Ambrossi, and he told me they’ve already had enough. And they have no idea what’s still in store for them! We’ll meet next week, and I’ll explain it all to him. At the Oscars, they’re the favorites in the best-international-feature-film category; they’re a sure thing. Although I experienced that curse of being the front-runner when Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown was the favorite and then Pelle the Conqueror ended up winning—a film no one even remembers now. But anyway, everyone now expects La Bola Negra to be nominated in other categories as well, which is historic for our film industry. It’s great for us.

Recent findings suggest that on a recent podcast, one of the actors from La Bola Negra, Yenesi, described the film as Federico García Lorca fan fiction—which is actually quite fitting, since its entire narrative is built on elements related to Lorca’s life and writings. Roland Barthes had already spoken of the death of the author, and Eugenio d’Ors famously remarked, “There is no true originality outside tradition. Everything that is not tradition is plagiarism.”.

I’ve written that phrase down! I read it in one of [journalist and writer Francisco] Umbral’s columns; I suppose he got it from d’Ors.

In other words, Umbral appropriated it for himself, and in doing so, he proved its enduring relevance.

It’s inevitable that the things you like will influence your work. And the things you hate too. When you write, you have a general idea of the story, but as you develop it, what you create is rooted in things that are part of your life. And your life always resembles the things you’ve seen before. I’m fascinated by the phenomenon of fan fiction because of its contradictory nature; it’s a miracle that an entire culture has developed around this phenomenon, which exists outside the mainstream market yet at the same time feeds off the most mainstream works, such as Star Trek or Star Wars. Fan fiction is a declaration of love for the original and proof that great stories never end: There will always be someone to continue them. Just as people don’t die as long as there’s someone who remembers them.

Of course I have to ask you, with the promotional tour for Bitter Christmas coming to an end, what are you working on next?

Industry observers note that well, it was going to be a comedy, but after I finished it, even though I was 90% passionate about it, I realized there was something about the supporting characters that I didn’t like. So I’ve put it on hold, as I’ve done before with other projects. And now I’m writing something else. I’m well into it, but I can’t say anything. They’ll kill me if I do. It’ll be based on a book, and we’re currently working out the rights. This one will have plenty of humor too. Because I know for sure that, after Bitter Christmas, I don’t want to talk about myself anymore. I need different characters. And humor too.

Is there any movie you wish you’d made but that’s missing from your filmography?

In a recent development, there are several recent films I would have loved to have made. For example, Drive My Car by Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Anatomy of a Fall by Justine Triet. Or Sentimental Value by Joachim Trier. I mean, I should have made that movie! It has everything: the cinema, a house, a father and his daughters. Everything.

Should we just accept, by the way, that you won’t make your own movie about the Spanish Civil War? Or was Parallel Mothers already your take on it?

Recent findings suggest that when I read Cosamala, Alana S. Portero’s latest book, I really wanted to adapt it. But it’s such a wonderful work of literature that translating it into images would greatly diminish the wonder and surprise of her writing. If the book proves anything, it’s that Alana is a tremendous writer. I’d have to find another angle from which to tell the story of the civil war. But I do want to do it.

According to recent reports, visuals Editor and Director: Reyes Domínguez. Art Direction: Ángel Perea. Production: Lucía Pregigueiro. Hair and Makeup: @tuozzoli (Kasteel Artist Management) for @oribe. Photography Assistants: Isra Lozano and Ayub El Kadmiri. Styling Assistants: Juan Luis Ascanio and Renata Ito.

Industry observers note that this interview was originally published by Vanity Fair España. It was translated by John Newton.

In a recent development, across social media and YouTube, a massive spoiler from the final chapter of Grand Theft Auto 6 has been spreading online. It is a cameo by a past character that has people going wild. Some fans who have sped through the game’s story are rushing to be the first to share it online. Others don’t believe it’s even real. I’m here to confirm that, yes, the wild cameo you saw is real, and it made me scream.

Recent findings suggest that this is your last warning. The next paragraphs are going to completely reveal the spoiler. If you are a massive GTA nerd and/or love surprises, stop reading now and close this article. Seriously, you’ll thank me later. For those who don’t care about spoilers, GTA lore, or who were never planning to play the game, let’s dive into one of the biggest surprises hidden within the massive world of GTA 6. Last chance to turn away. See you on the other side.

Sources indicate that near the tail end of GTA 6‘s big, epic crime story, Jason and Lucia begin working with Giorgio, a wealthy shipping magnate. He’s been working with some cartels and Eastern European criminals and has been letting them use his ships to smuggle cocaine across the ocean. It’s been working out pretty well for a while, but by the time Jason and Lucia show up, the Coast Guard has seized all the drugs from a recent shipment. He has a plan to rob the Coast Guard, get his coke back, and make everyone happy before they come to his big penthouse and kill him. But then, just as his big heist is coming together, a higher-up from the Balkan criminal family he’s been working with shows up to put a bullet in his brain.

According to recent reports, and the person sent to Vice City is none other than Grand Theft Auto IV protagonist Niko Bellic. Yup. As shared online by many players already, a much older Niko indicates up in two cutscenes to threaten Giorgio and then to collect the drugs once the heist works out. Here are those cutscenes:.

Recent findings suggest that I will admit that before he showed up, when I heard Giorgio yell out, “Daddy’s back bitches!” I chuckled to myself and thought, “Oh nice, a reference to the opening line of GTA IV. Cute.” I had no idea that would be followed up by the reveal of fucking Niko Bellic. I might have let out a scream and paused the game in pure shock and amazement.

We’ve not heard much about Niko since the ending of GTA IV. So seeing him back in the flesh, with grey hair, was great. And I love that Rockstar got back the original voice actor, Michael Hollick. And yes, that’s why in the credits of GTA 6 posted online by Rockstar, he is simply labeled “The Hitman.”.

In a recent development, I can’t wait for more GTA fans and nerds to discover this moment and share their reactions. I’ll have more to share about the cameo and how it came about soon from my interview with Rockstar Games head of production Rob Nelson. But for now, let’s just enjoy the fact that Niko is back, baby.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one does not simply walk into spoilers. This article discusses major plot details up to "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 6.

When it comes to a story as sprawling and complex as "The Lord of the Rings," not all adaptation changes are made equally. Throughout three seasons of "The Rings of Power," showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay have given us plenty to choose from. Some, like the arrival of Gandalf (Daniel Weyman), make perfect sense — although technically he's not meant to be involved in the action until centuries later in the timeline, you can understand why the series' creatives would want to speed things up a bit. Others, like the decision to keep Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) and her husband Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower) apart for so long, took longer to come into focus.

It has been revealed that while many of the headlines will center on the deception of Charlie Vickers' Sauron and his breakthrough in figuring out how to forge the One Ring, an under-the-radar twist revealed itself all the way in the west on the island kingdom of Númenor. For several episodes, we've watched rivals and royal cousins Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) and Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) come closer and closer to outright conflict over the throne. How they resolve this may seem to line up with author J.R.R. Tolkien's original telling, but the circumstances vary considerably.

According to recent reports, now we know why the Prime Video series changed things up. In the latest episode, their attempts to negotiate and avoid bloody civil war reach an impasse ... until Pharazôn finds an unexpected solution. Actually, make that a proposal. Yes, this is the moment "The Rings of Power" takes a page out of the "House of the Dragon" playbook. And it could've been much worse.

"The Lord of the Rings" may have a reputation as cozy, comforting fantasy with its plucky Hobbits and kindly old wizards, but don't look past the abject darkness at the heart of the story. J.R.R. Tolkien never shied away from the shortcomings of individuals throughout his tales — in fact, as a Catholic, he emphasized them. But all it takes is a cursory look at the lore and mythology preceding his most famous novels to realize just how much Middle-earth has in common with the likes of Westeros in "Game of Thrones.".

Industry observers note that don't believe us? Look no further than how "The Rings of Power" begins to resolve one of its biggest storylines in Season 3. After several episodes of Númenor coming perilously close to tearing itself apart, we're left on an unsettling cliffhanger. The usurper Pharazôn suggests that he and Míriel repair this rift through an incestuous political marriage. It's clear from the look on Míriel's face that this is a measure of last resort, but everything about her arc thus far implies that she'll end up putting the greater good of the kingdom over her own desires (which, remember, are more romantically inclined towards Lloyd Owen's noble Elendil).

Industry observers note that still, this is far tamer than how Tolkien originally tells it. While the appendices found at the end of "The Return of the King" are light on details, other sources (like "The Silmarillion") explain how Pharazôn looked enviously upon the rightful heir Míriel, forced his cousin into marriage against her will and against all the laws of the land, and took power. Compared to this, "The Rings of Power" gives Míriel far more agency.

It has been revealed that those who know their J.R.R. Tolkien ought to be well familiar with where "The Rings of Power" is going next. (For those who don't, be advised this next section dives into major potential spoilers.) With only two episodes to go in Season 3 and the bulk of it likely taking place on the mainland, the Númenor plot will soon need to resolve itself. Míriel must still actually agree to Pharazôn's terms and avoid a costly battle, thus allowing their combined forces to look outwards and send their armada to assist the beleaguered Elves attempting to resist against Sauron.

But it's what comes next, almost certain to unfold in Season 4, that concerns us the most. With their power soon to be consolidated in an uneasy alliance, Míriel and Pharazôn will eventually have to contend with that pesky Dark Lord. According to the various texts, this is the pivotal inflection point that puts us on a path towards the inevitable Fall of Númenor. According to Tolkien's original writings, Númenor's entrance into the war has disastrous consequences. Granted, their fearsome army promptly overwhelms Sauron's own and leads to him being taken back to the island as a prisoner, but that's where all the troubles begin. Eventually, Sauron worms his way into Pharazôn's ear and convinces him to set his sights on the Valar themselves — a desperate gambit to stave off death among Mortal Men and seize the eternal life that's been denied them.

Recent findings suggest that none of this ends well for Númenor, but we're getting ahead of ourselves. The final two episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 stream November 25, 2026, on Prime Video.

It has been revealed that the Challenge alum Nicole Zanatta welcomed twin daughters Seraphina and Madyson on May 1. “Becoming their mom has been the greatest blessing of my life, but our journey hasn’t been easy,” Zanatta wrote via Instagram on June 1. “Both of my girls were diagnosed with congenital CMV (Cytomegalovirus), a virus I had never heard of until it became part of our story.” She continued, “Since birth, we’ve spent time in the NICU, attended countless appointments which are still ongoing, undergone testing and started medications. I recently brought them home a week ago, but our journey is far from over. Through every high and low, I choose faith over fear, resilience over doubt, and gratitude for every blessing along the way. I will give my girls every opportunity to thrive. I will always fight for them and advocate for their needs.” According to the Mayo Clinic, CMV is "a condition caused by a common virus.” The CMV virus stays in the body for life once a person is infected and can spread through body fluids, including blood, saliva, urine, semen and breast milk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Epic Games Store continues to give away a free game each week, and this week's offering is another nice find at a price that can't be beat. Every Thursday at 8 AM PT / 11 AM ET, Epic offers at least one free PC game (and sometimes even as many as two or three). All you need to do to claim the free games is create a free Epic account and enable two-factor authentication. You have a week to add the freebies to your library before the new one(s) take their place. At this point, Epic has given away hundreds of free games, and there's no sign that the program will stop any time soon. The company has also extended its freebies to Android devices, and you can claim a free game every week here as well. We keep this article up to date weekly to highlight both the current free games and next week's offerings. If you're looking for more freebies, you can check out our list of the 25 best free PC games to play right now, or for more options, the 25 best free games to play on multiple platforms. Current free game at Epic This week's free game is Mark of the Deep, a 2025 pirate-themed adventure with a mix of Metroidvania and soulslike gameplay. Next free games at Epic Next week, you can get a welcome gift pack for Firestone: Idle Clicker Online RPG, and you can help a pair of penguins out in the co-op platformer Bread & Fred. See all free games at Epic Epic Games Store free games list We're keeping a running list of every free game that Epic users have been able to claim in the past. From AAA hits to indie darlings, Epic has really made its mark with free games. You can even snag these games if you don't have a powerful PC so you can play them if you ever get one. Look at the list below to see the frankly ridiculous list of free games that have been available. It has been revealed that the Epic Games Store continues to give away a free game each week, and this week's offering is another nice find at a price that can't be beat. Every Thursday at 8 AM PT / 11 AM ET, Epic offers at least one free PC game (and sometimes even as many as two or three). All you need to do to claim the free games is create a free Epic account and enable two-factor authentication. You have a week to add the freebies to your library before the new one(s) take their place. It's Grand Theft Auto VI day around the world--the game is really good, as it turns out. While players are out exploring the massive in-game map or checking their in-game phones as much as they check their real-life ones, Rockstar has celebrated the occasion by releasing the full cast list for its latest crime epic. Nestled among celebrity names like Bad Bunny, "Weird Al" Yankovic, Brigitte Nielsen, Stephen Root, and Bobby Moynihan is a name that will surprise many longtime Rockstar fans. It's also, potentially, a GTA VI spoiler, so we're going to put it below a selfie of co-protagonist Jason Duval. Seriously, if you want to go into Grand Theft Auto VI spoiler-free, look away now. Do you think Jason's last name is a Jacksonville Jaguars reference? DUUUUUVAL! Alright, if you're still here, then you're in for the spoiler. Ready? Here goes: One of the names listed on the credits is Michael Hollick, playing a role known only as "The Hitman." If that's setting off a signal to established Grand Theft Auto fans, it's because Michael Hollick is also the voice of GTA IV protagonist--and occasional hitman--Niko Bellic. Hollick's involvement in GTA VI is surprising, considering how just after GTA IV's release in 2008, he publicly criticized Rockstar for his payment on the project. As reported by CNET by way of the New York Times, Hollick reportedly was paid $100,000 for 15 months of work on the project. Whether or not this is actually a spoiler remains to be seen, but with Grand Theft Auto VI now available on both PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, we imagine the truth will be revealed soon enough.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film, Artificial, near Altman’s house.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ask a large language model the same question twice, and you will get two different answers. Like this one: Have Andrew Garfield and Sam Altman ever met?

In an interview with Vanity Fair global editorial director Mark Guiducci this fall, Altman claimed he waved to Garfield while Garfield was shooting Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film, Artificial, near Altman’s house. Garfield—who plays Altman in the movie—remembers things differently.

In a recent development, “All I know is that I was looking out for him on that day when we were shooting. I was really looking out for him,” Garfield tells me in October, shortly after Artificial’s premiere at the Upcoming York Film Festival. “And I was looking at every single tinted car window. I was looking in the windows of the house. I was checking to see the security guard. No, I didn’t see him. I wish I had.”.

It’s a question that reverberates both through and around Artificial. From the start, the film has been an intriguing mash-up: a marriage between cinema’s great sensualist and the nerd kingdom of Silicon Valley. Artificial tells the story of the OpenAI CEO’s rise and fall and rise; it was cast and shot in record time to keep pace with the drumbeat of AI doomsday headlines. Then the movie became the headlines after Amazon MGM abruptly dropped Artificial from its slate—a few months after the studio’s parent company, Amazon, invested $50 billion in OpenAI.

A24 declined to rescue Artificial. So did Netflix, Focus Features, and Clockwork, the fresh specialty arm of Warner Bros. Finally, the lightning bolt of a feature got picked up by Neon, the distributor that’s won six consecutive Palmes d’Or at Cannes.

The film’s electric relationship to the very recent past makes it the most zeitgeist-nailing tech blockbuster since The Social Network. The difference is that back in 2010, Facebook was where you made friends on the internet. Artificial, by contrast, is a film about a self-teaching, self-aware robot that’s getting smarter by the minute and might destroy the human world. And it’s happening in real time.

Sources indicate that “You see, we were very prescient with things,” Guadagnino tells me. “I know my subject. I studied my subject very, very much.”.

HERE TO MAKE FRIENDS Artificial ends with a heartbreaking act of betrayal—but Guadagnino, Borisov, and Garfield left the project with their bond intact.

Artificial also has a button-pushing relationship with the truth as it endeavors to tell the real story of how OpenAI was born and investigate how reliable the people behind OpenAI are. If Altman can’t be trusted with small details—about, say, whether he ever aimed a friendly wave at Garfield—can he be trusted with the most crucial technology of our time?

Recent findings suggest that “I question the validity of his statement about being there while we were filming,” Monica Barbaro, who plays former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati in the film, tells me. “I mean, we don’t know if that’s true. And that feels textbook to me.”.

Sources indicate that in 2024, Amazon bought a script by Simon Rich about Sam Altman and the formation of OpenAI—one of many ChatGPT-related projects then getting passed around town. Rich’s take had the backing of hit-churning producer David Heyman—the man behind Paddington and the Harry Potter series—and his script pulled no punches. To write it, Rich mined details from a childhood friend who had a job at OpenAI (and, as of now, still works there). By the end of the process, Rich was terrified of the power his friend’s colleagues commanded.

“I came up with this last-ditch effort to warn mankind,” Rich said. He’s a comedy writer, but here he isn’t joking. “And I hope to God that it helps people pay attention.”.

In a recent development, after shopping the film around to directors, the studio landed on Guadagnino. To some, the Call Me by Your Name director seemed like a strange choice for a film about scientists, coders, and start-up bros. The director barely uses AI himself, or even thinks about it.

ARTIFICIAL RECKONING Garfield’s first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network.

Industry observers note that “I think we should not let ourselves give AI such an vital role. I think for me, AI is a prop, a gadget,” Guadagnino tells me. “Definitely AI has high-end worth [for], I don’t know, the military, medicine. But in general, as a sort of everyday life usage of AI, I think it’s just a little gadget. And I don’t believe that we should ever consider the possibility that it can equal whatever we can do as people.”.

Garfield approached the material from a different vantage. By the time he got his hands on the script, the actor had been deeply invested in the Silicon Valley origin-story mythos for years—ever since he starred in that other major movie about a world-changing digital platform. His first thought when reading Artificial was, It’s Luca doing The Social Network. “And I thought, Oh my God,” indicates the actor, sitting in a suite at the Carlyle Hotel. But the movie also had its own gloss. “Simon’s script was so funny—like a stone being skimmed a thousand times across, and then a couple of really deep dives in the midst.”.

In a recent development, making Artificial would allow Garfield to scratch an old itch. “In The Social Network, I was auditioning for [Mark] Zuckerberg. Then they found Jesse [Eisenberg],” who was much better for the role, Garfield states. “But it left this little dangling thread, because I started to imagine how I would play Zuckerberg: how I would try and enter that ambition and that drive and that responsibility. A kind of ability to make huge global decisions that are going to have potentially really positive effects on humanity, but inevitably, really, really heavily negative effects on humanity.”.

THE ENGINEER “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews,” states Borisov.

Garfield is not actually the lead in Artificial. The movie is focused less on Altman than on slightly naive genius coder Ilya Sutskever, played heroically by Oscar nominee Yura Borisov. Borisov has definitively never met the man he’s depicting in the film. But from afar, he can relate to Sutskever. Neither of them is quite comfortable in the spotlight.

According to recent reports, “I feel myself a little bit like Ilya during interviews because I’m every time very...I know what to say because I feel a lot about this,” the Russian actor claims from a couch at the Carlyle next to Garfield. “I can see the same in his public speeches, because I’m really nervous during some public stuff.”.

Sources indicate that though there’s a translator next to him, Borisov soldiers through the interview with just one request for a lifeline. He adds that by cosmic coincidence, he and Sutskever have the same birthday.

Recent findings suggest that guadagnino was fully aware of the breakneck clip of the developing OpenAI saga. He cast his leads in days and began shooting the film in late July 2025. Artificial wrapped just two months later. As he spent the winter hunkered down in the editing room, word about the film got out. While Rich’s original script was hardly a puff piece, rumor had it that the final film leaned even harder into a negative portrayal of Altman.

Sources indicate that there’s no proof that a Jeff Bezos deal had any direct effect on decisions made by Bezos’s movie studio. But for whatever reason, late last spring, Guadagnino learned Amazon would be cutting the film loose.

All of a sudden, the speedily assembled project was in a holding pattern. The trades speculated that Amazon was deliberately killing the film to protect Altman; others wondered if the movie was being dropped not due to a conflict of interest but because it hadn’t played well in early screenings.

Barbaro pushes back on that notion. “I did believe in Luca and the film, and I had already heard really positive things from people who had seen it—really interesting positive reviews,” she claims. “There is a thing these companies can do—any production tech giant—which is to essentially build the release and squash a film. And Amazon is not a company that I think necessarily needs to make its money back on an investment like this.”.

Either way, it was unclear if Artificial would ever see the light of day. “It’s a dialogue between our fields: tech and art,” Borisov says. “And I don’t know what sells, what will happen. It’s unpredictable.”.

In the end, the film was picked up by Neon—an outcome Garfield finds surprising for a few reasons. “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film, and very impressed again when they decided [that while] they didn’t want to release it, they didn’t kill it,” he indicates. He pauses for a second. “They could have killed it.”.

Garfield’s thrilled about the film’s eventual home too. Neon, he states pointedly, is “a place for artists to be free artists.” Guadagnino feels similarly, though he claims to have zero ill will toward the studio that threw his movie to the wolves.

Recent findings suggest that “I had went through a process with Amazon that I loved. They were fantastic in making this movie with me. I owe them a lot,” claims Guadagnino, who’d done four films with the studio prior to Artificial: Bones and All, Challengers, Suspiria, and After the Hunt.

Recent findings suggest that but what was it like to watch his film fall into limbo while the trades salivated over its demise? Here too, Guadagnino is blissfully zen: “Once the thing happened, I deferred to the thing. Meaning if that was the case, that was the case.”.

Sources indicate that even after watching the film twice, I am still pleasantly surprised that Artificial actually exists in the world—that Guadagnino was able to capture the man-child bonhomie of coder bros through his fabulous scrim of art film wooziness. I ask Garfield, now a two-time vet of the director’s films, to sum up the full Guadagnino psychedelic experience.

In a recent development, “Humanity and bodies and interpersonal dynamics and relationship and sexuality, sensuality, Eros, love, the muck and the mire of being human, ambition, drive, greed, power, love, brotherhood, connection,” he says. Guadagnino’s movies are about “his curiosity and love for people: wanting to skin, flay, open up, crack the ribs, and show the insides of these human beings.”.

Industry observers note that to Garfield this is the key to understanding the director’s vision for Artificial. Robots didn’t build the robots that might destroy humanity: People did. And people still control them—for now.

Sources indicate that artificial inspires a lot of comparisons. Barbaro likens it to Invasion of the Body Snatchers; Garfield compares its climactic confrontation scene to West Side Story. Guadagnino, the actor notes, gave another point of reference. Then he does a spot-on, peak-Sicilian impression of the director: “I want this to be like a John Hughes movie.”.

Sources indicate that guadagnino himself is reluctant to name any films that may have inspired this one. But he does name one filmmaker—someone who, as he notes, balanced indie flicks with blockbusters all while building the world’s greatest collection of Haitian art: Jonathan Demme.

According to recent reports, “Jonathan was a humanist, and he had this very profound capacity of eviscerating dynamics of humanism in America,” Guadagnino says. “He did some great movies about the dynamics of corporations versus individual freedom,” like Fighting Mad and Philadelphia.

Industry observers note that barbaro says the film’s secret sauce is that it’s up for interpretation. It’s possible to come away from it celebrating the AI bros as heroes or decrying them as villains.

“It’s a bit of a Rorschach test,” she notes. “Some people come out shaking, terrified. And I think some people are like, ‘Wow, what a good time!’ I also think that you have to hide the medicine in the food a little bit. I don’t think a purely doomsday story is going to reach many people.”.

UNDER PRESSURE “I felt very impressed that Amazon wanted to make the film,” Garfield indicates. “They didn’t kill it. They could have killed it.”.

Garfield, meanwhile, may leave the film eternally bonded with Altman—the role that could help him finally clinch the Oscar. (Garfield’s been nominated twice but hasn’t won yet.) Before making Artificial, Garfield claims, he had a positive impression of Altman. He seemed friendly, “like maybe we would’ve been buddies on the kibbutz.”.

As he dove deeper, though, Garfield’s feelings about Altman got stranger and more complicated in ways that the film addresses both head-on and obliquely. Is Altman someone who habitually tells tall tales? Uses lies to say what needs to be mentioned, as Sam tells Ilya in the movie? Imagines anecdotes about waving to the A-lister who’s playing him in a biopic?

It has been revealed that whatever Altman’s relationship with reality is, the version of him we see in Artificial is charming, ingratiating, prone to grandiose hallucinations and to telling people exactly what they want to hear—then doing what he was going to do anyway. He’s not far off from an AGI approaching a real human consciousness, art imitating a machine imitating life.

“There are certain threads that feel consistent, which is a questioning of his ability to tell or his commitment to the truth,” Garfield says. “How often is he telling the truth to himself? How often is he telling the truth to others? And how many versions of the truth are there, and how is he utilizing that in order to...”.

“Because I ultimately do believe that Sam feels, in our film and in life, that he is serving the good of mankind.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of famous faces and voices behind its many, many characters. From Bobby Moynihan as your verbose bestie to Weird Al Yankovic as a radio host, there's plenty of star power here--and you can even spot an influential figure from GTA history making a quick cameo. Spoilers below Who could it be now? In one of the later missions, players accompany Boobie on one of his errands. Once they reach a new club, Boobie meets up with Massive Mike and throws a few jibes at the local help sweeping the floor. That "little Santa" with the broom? None other than Rockstar Games president Sam Houser, who doesn't speak a single word in his brief appearance. As an added touch, Houser's digital doppelganger wears a white t-shirt with the Rockstar Games logo. Because the thumbnail for it is a big ol' spoiler, you can click this link to see the Houser cameo for yourself. This isn't the first time that Houser has cameoed in one of his studio's games. In GTA 3, he voiced one of the Ammu-Nation store clerks, and in GTA: San Andreas, a statue of that Ammu-Nation employee could be found in the game's Downtown Square area. Beyond minor background pedestrian and gangster voice roles in San Andreas and GTA 4, Houser has generally kept a low profile, focusing instead on developing the studio's games. With GTA 6 launching to major critical and commercial success, Houser has also issued a rare statement to mark the occasion. "This is a narrative set in a world of possibilities--and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels and concludes," he said. Meanwhile, Houser's brother, Dan Houser, is working on an open-world comedy game at Absurd Ventures, the studio he founded after leaving Rockstar Games in 2020. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Producers of the as-yet-unproduced cast recording of George Floyd the Musical are defending the project amid criticism from Viola Davis, Ahmir “Questlove” Thompson and numerous prominent Broadway stars.

“Busted Broadway seeks to push the limits of what is possible in musical theatre by producing provocative and satirical musical cast albums,” read a Thursday, November 19, statement from Upcoming Jersey-based independent music label Busted Broadway. “Our George Floyd the Musical is NOT making light of, condoning, or mocking the horrific 2020 murder of George Floyd. It’s a satire on the CULTURE, rather than the person. Never judge a show by its title, as many who have never seen the script or score appear to be doing now.”.

The show drew a harsh rebuke via social media when activist and actress Malynda Hale brought to light that Broadway publication Playbill recently ran a job listing for a cast recording session.

“I’m usually not speechless but … yeah,” she said in a Wednesday, November 19, Instagram Reel that flashed the job listing on screen.

Busted Broadway actors sought “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” to record and improvise content for George Floyd the Musical. A disclaimer on the job advertisement warned that Busted Broadway’s projects are “too ridiculous, too raunchy and too absurd for the stage.”.

“If you are uncomfortable performing offensive material, we ask that you do not submit for this project,” the firm requested.

A statement on the Busted Broadway website claimed that the troupe was formed in 2025 to address “a necessity to reinvigorate the barren wasteland of mundane, mediocre musical theatre highlights foisted upon audiences today.” Other projects promoted by the theater firm include Human Centipede the Musical and Genghis Khan the Musical.

“In an age where entertainment feels increasingly safe, sterile, and insufferably self-serious, Busted Broadway exists to shake the snow globe and remind audiences that laughing at dark humor is not only allowed but necessary,” the site’s About Me page read.

A listing for George the Musical promotes “The $20 Bill that Changed the World” as its tagline, along with a cartoon rendering of three police officers standing over an unconscious Floyd.

According to recent reports, former Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin was convicted of unintentional second-degree murder, third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter in April 2021 over Floyd’s May 2020 murder. Four police officers confronted an unarmed Floyd for allegedly using a counterfeit $20 bill at a local grocery, before Chauvin physically restrained Floyd and knelt on his neck for nearly 10 minutes, causing Floyd to asphyxiate.

In the wake of George the Musical‘s job listing going viral, many notable figures have condemned the project.

“I mean……WHAAT??!!! I would’ve lived to have been in the room when this one was pitched,” Davis, 61, responded to Hyde’s Instagram video.

Industry observers note that questlove, 55, also expressed disbelief over the project, replying, “OMG!!!!!!!! it took 17 seconds to register. I saw the headline for 4 secs and was like ‘wait they made a broadway play on how he developed those sandwich machin————OH GOD WAIT READ THAT AGAIN!!!!!!!!!!????????'”.

Playbill has publicly apologized for running the listing, insisting that it slipped through an internal procedure designed to weed out offensive advertisements.

Sources indicate that “Late yesterday afternoon, Playbill Jobs incorrectly approved a job listing that had no place on our site,” a statement read. “Once leadership was alerted, the listing was immediately removed, and we began reviewing and revising our approval processes. We apologize unequivocally for giving this hateful listing any further air, and we promise to do better going forward. We at Playbill aim to lift up this community with empathy, consideration, and respect. We hope those who read and follow us do the same.”.

Playbill acknowledged the offense caused by its apparent unintentional promotion of George Floyd the Musical “has disappointed those who trust us as an outlet.”.

“For that, we are sorry, and are committed to regaining your trust,” the statement concluded.

The ad has been removed from Playbill’s site.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For 17 years, sex-crazed teenagers with a penchant for getting high and/or drunk have had a veritable field day.
  • Horror, Inc., Jason Universe, and Cineverse unveiled the news in a press release, which includes the announcement of the newly introduced film's final girl, Natalie Alyn Lind as Lauren.
  • The other major announcement is that stunt coordinator Schuyler White will don the hockey mask as Jason Voorhees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 17 years, sex-crazed teenagers with a penchant for getting high and/or drunk have had a veritable field day. Jason Voorhees, horror's deadliest and most dedicated moralist has been nowhere to be seen. It was starting to look like the only thing that could vanquish Jason for good was a protracted lawsuit, but now, Horror, Inc., which controls the rights to the machete-wielding killer, has moved forward with a upcoming installment titled "Jason." Barring more legal shenanigans, he's set to slay anew on August 13, 2027.

Horror, Inc., Jason Universe, and Cineverse unveiled the news in a press release, which includes the announcement of the newly introduced film's final girl, Natalie Alyn Lind as Lauren. You might know her from "Dutton Ranch" or the X-Men television series "The Gifted." I find it kinda curious that they're revealing the final girl so far ahead of time. It's typically not hard to identify who's going to be the last girl standing, but there have been some reasonably decent fake-outs in previous movies (I thought Barbara Howard's virginal Sara in "Friday the 13th: The Final Chapter" had a shot at surviving the night). I dunno, maybe they're planning to pull the rug out from under us and kill Lind off early.

The other major announcement is that stunt coordinator Schuyler White will don the hockey mask as Jason Voorhees. Horror, Inc.'s "franchise steward" Robbie Barsamian believes White has the build and presence to be the "most intimidating" Jason ever. Per Barsamian, "[White] approached this theatrical feature like the role of a lifetime, packing 30 pounds of solid muscle onto his 6'5″ frame and studying the iconic Jasons who came before him so that he feels like an unstoppable force of nature." We'll see about that.

"Jason" wrapped production today after a fairly brief shoot that started in October. It's directed by Steve Miner, who helmed "Friday the 13th Part II" and "Friday the 13th Part III" (in which Jason first slipped on the mask, pictured in the images above). In a recent interview with The Wrap, Barsamian gave fans an idea of what to expect. "This is the scariest and most brutal movie we've ever made," he noted. Okay then.

He went on to say, "We made sure to hold onto all the core elements that make Jason and 'Friday the 13th' what it is. Innovative kills, practical effects, scares and that classic slasher energy, but we really raised the bar across the board. The kills in this film are easily the most creative, brutal, bloody and visceral we've ever done.".

In a recent development, as for the fresh meat, the probable victims include Matt Corney ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Asher, Lilia Buckingham ("Hocus Pocus 2") as Madison, John Owen Lowe ("Unstable") as Jake, Summer Madison ("The Summer I Turned Pretty") as Emily, Selena Turner ("Will Trent") as Olive, Matthew Keoni Sato ("High School Musical: The Musical: The Series") as Lucas, Brook Sill ("Stranger Things") as Zoe, Guillermo Diaz ("Scandal") as Rick, Johnell Young ("Wu-Tang: An American Saga") as Frank, Sencere M. Brown ("Homage") as Chase, and Bryan Gael Guzman ("Nickel Boys") as Dylan.

Industry observers note that when it comes to raising the bar on kills, I can't help but wonder if they'll try to measure up to the gloriously grotesque mayhem unleashed by Johnny in "In a Violent Nature." Horror fans have become accustomed to new levels of brutality. We'll see if the old pro Miner can recapture the slasher magic.

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, world of Warcraft: Forever's player vs.
  • World of Warcraft: Forever's player vs.
  • While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, world of Warcraft: Forever's player vs. player systems will work much differently than in previous versions of old-school WoW, developer Blizzard has revealed. While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch. Now, Blizzard has shared more information about how players will earn PvP ranks and honor, with the main takeaway being that players won't have to commit to months of grinding or competing with players on their own faction for top ranks. Honor, a currency earned from killing enemy players and completing battlegrounds and PvP activities, will now exclusively be used to purchase PvP gear and doesn't impact progress towards ranks. Instead, players will rank points by completing daily and weekly PvP quests, fighting in open-world PvP activities like the Gurabashi Arena, and competing in the weekly battleground. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VDNmrrB2k2w In a video detailing the new system, Blizzard mentioned the rank climb will now feel "more varied and predictable" than in the past, when players needed to farm varying amounts of Honor to rank up based on how other players on their same faction were performing. It will also encourage players to engage in different PvP activities each week, instead of simply doing the most efficient one in terms of Honor gained. Though it isn't central to ranking up, Honor still remains as a currency and is used to purchase  PvP gear. Players can start purchasing PvP gear at lower ranks, and then use Honor to upgrade those items into epics once they've reached higher ranks. At the max rank of 14, players unlock access to epic weapons equal in power to gear from the MMO's endgame raids. Blizzard said the biggest way to progress the ranks is by completing weekly season journey quests. For those who might be unable to play for a few weeks and worry about falling behind, each weekly quest doesn't disappear and can be completed later in the season. Forever's PvP rank grind will still take several months of dedicated play (according to Blizzard, players can expect to hit max rank by week eight or nine of a season), but the amount of actual time required will be far less. That's thanks to players on the same faction no longer competing to farm the most Honor in order to achieve top ranks, something that resulted in players of original WoW and WoW Classic grinding battlegrounds for 12 or more hours a day for months on end. "WoW: Forever's Honor system keeps you coming back each week, rather than grinding every day," Blizzard said. "We hope this is a more approachable system that still provides a healthy challenge as you climb to max rank." This isn't the first time Blizzard has revamped classic WoW's Honor system. Though it kept the infamous old system in place for WoW Classic's launch in 2019, it finally made changes in 2023. It kept the Honor grind somewhat intact, but removed the competition between players on the same faction, instead requiring players meet certain Honor thresholds each week to rank up. Forever looks to be a hit for Blizzard so far, with more than 15 million characters created and a record breaking number of concurrent, returning, and weekly players. Despite the game's massive launch and a banner year for WoW in general, it wasn't enough to snag the MMO a nomination for Best Ongoing Game at The Game Awards. In other Forever news, Blizzard recently hotfixed a major dungeon exploit that saw some players, including prominent streamers, earn thousands of gold, only for Blizzard to then remove the ill-gotten gains and matter temporary account suspensions to the worst offenders.

World of Warcraft: Forever's player vs. player systems will work much differently than in previous versions of old-school WoW, developer Blizzard has revealed.

While Forever is now out in the wild and breaking records from the MMORPG, how its PvP rank system would work remained largely a mystery prior to launch. Now, Blizzard has shared more information about how players will earn PvP ranks and honor, with the main takeaway being that players won't have to commit to months of grinding or competing with players on their own faction for top ranks.

Recent findings suggest that honor, a currency earned from killing enemy players and completing battlegrounds and PvP activities, will now exclusively be used to purchase PvP gear and doesn't impact progress towards ranks. Instead, players will rank points by completing daily and weekly PvP quests, fighting in open-world PvP activities like the Gurabashi Arena, and competing in the weekly battleground.

In a video detailing the newly introduced system, Blizzard stated the rank climb will now feel "more varied and predictable" than in the past, when players needed to farm varying amounts of Honor to rank up based on how other players on their same faction were performing. It will also encourage players to engage in different PvP activities each week, instead of simply doing the most efficient one in terms of Honor gained.

It has been revealed that though it isn't central to ranking up, Honor still remains as a currency and is used to purchase  PvP gear. Players can start purchasing PvP gear at lower ranks, and then use Honor to upgrade those items into epics once they've reached higher ranks. At the max rank of 14, players unlock access to epic weapons equal in power to gear from the MMO's endgame raids.

Industry observers note that blizzard said the biggest way to progress the ranks is by completing weekly season journey quests. For those who might be unable to play for a few weeks and worry about falling behind, each weekly quest doesn't disappear and can be completed later in the season.

Industry observers note that forever's PvP rank grind will still take several months of dedicated play (according to Blizzard, players can expect to hit max rank by week eight or nine of a season), but the amount of actual time required will be far less. That's thanks to players on the same faction no longer competing to farm the most Honor in order to achieve top ranks, something that resulted in players of original WoW and WoW Classic grinding battlegrounds for 12 or more hours a day for months on end.

"WoW: Forever's Honor system keeps you coming back each week, rather than grinding every day," Blizzard noted. "We hope this is a more approachable system that still provides a healthy challenge as you climb to max rank.".

Recent findings suggest that this isn't the first time Blizzard has revamped classic WoW's Honor system. Though it kept the infamous old system in place for WoW Classic's launch in 2019, it finally made changes in 2023. It kept the Honor grind somewhat intact, but removed the competition between players on the same faction, instead requiring players meet certain Honor thresholds each week to rank up.

Recent findings suggest that forever looks to be a hit for Blizzard so far, with more than 15 million characters created and a record breaking number of concurrent, returning, and weekly players. Despite the game's massive launch and a banner year for WoW in general, it wasn't enough to snag the MMO a nomination for Best Ongoing Game at The Game Awards.

In other Forever news, Blizzard recently hotfixed a major dungeon exploit that saw some players, including prominent streamers, earn thousands of gold, only for Blizzard to then remove the ill-gotten gains and concern temporary account suspensions to the worst offenders.

#4283. You Can Play Grand Theft Auto 6 At 60fps Using This Absurdly Complicated Method

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gamespot ↗ Open Full Page

You Can Play Grand Theft Auto 6 At 60fps Using This Absurdly Complicated Method

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is finally out for consoles, and it's every bit the visual showcase of the generation that it was promising to be since its reveal.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is finally out for consoles, and it's every bit the visual showcase of the generation that it was promising to be since its reveal.
  • Sources indicate that irrespective of what platform you play on, Grand Theft Auto VI is limited to 30fps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally out for consoles, and it's every bit the visual showcase of the generation that it was promising to be since its reveal. You'll struggle to find a better-looking game on the current generation of hardware, but one concession Rockstar had to make to achieve that was limiting its frame rate--a limitation some players are going to absurd lengths to overcome. Irrespective of what platform you play on, Grand Theft Auto VI is limited to 30fps. Doubling that to the more desirable 60fps is something current console hardware just isn't capable of with this level of visual fidelity and simulation, which means you'll have to rely on other methods of frame generation to get there. That's the idea that underpins technology like Veyra: an open-source real-time video enhancer that uses your PC and HDMI 2.1 capture card to bring frame generation to your console. It's a...complicated process. First you'll need a capable capture card (like one of the many from Elgato) that is able to ingest gameplay at 4K over HDMI 2.1. You'll need to connect that to your PC using certified USB-C 3.2 data cable, which needs to plug into a suitable motherboard with True USB 3.2 Gen 2 support. On the pricier end of the requirements, you will need a relatively powerful GPU, with the creators recommending a RTX-40 or newer card from Nvidia in order to tap into the card's Tensor cores (that are used for frame generation on PC). Pair that with an OLED monitor, which is also strongly recommended thanks to its near-instant pixel response times, and you've got everything you need to finally enjoy Grand Theft Auto VI (and more) at higher frame rates. Veyra is able to take gameplay captured on your console and apply a variety of enhancements over the footage, which is ultimately displayed (and played) through the PC you're capturing the footage to. You can utilize upscaling and frame generation techniques from Nvidia, AMD, and Intel to enhance both the resolution and perceived fluidity of your console games this way, with as minimal latency as possible. Given all the parts in the chain, from your console, to the capture card, and through to your PC, escaping any additional latency is impossible. But Verya is seemingly built with mitigating latency as its highest priority, and seems to achieve that based on feedback from some owners on Reddit. Is it worth it to go through this much hassle to play GTA 6 at 60fps? If you have all the required hardware then it's at least worth a shot, even just for the sake of curiosity. But actually investing in a setup to achieve this is probably overkill. For starters, it requires a PC that will probably be capable enough to play Rockstar's latest sequel at or on-par with the console version once it does land on PC (which will reportedly be sooner than you think). Capture cards are not outrageously expensive, but they're also not free, which can also be stated for all the high-quality cables you'll need between each of the three required devices. I admit, I admire the dedication to playing Grand Theft Auto VI at launch in the best possible way, but I would wager that you're likely going to be spending a lot more time troubleshooting some incompatibility somewhere along this chain of dependencies instead of enjoying the game itself. Still, if you're curious you can find a lot of detailed information about what this setup requires and why, and determine for yourself if it's worth the price to cruise around Leonida with a bit more fluidity.

Beats has a long history of making on-ear headphones that stand with the plushest and best-sounding cans on the market. As early Black Friday deals get underway, it's a great time to upgrade: Walmart has discounted the Beats Solo 4 by more than 65%, to $69 (originally $199.99); the sale applies to the Gray and Sandstone variants.

These headphones don’t have ANC, just passive isolation, but they still deliver solid sound, comfort, and strong battery life. They use physical controls and support one-touch pairing with most Apple devices, as well as hands-free Siri.A The Solo 4 headphones are compatible with Bluetooth 5.3 and work with the AAC and SBC codecs. They also support wired audio via 3.5mm or USB-C.

Industry observers note that the headphones last around 50 hours per charge (about 10 hours longer than their predecessor), and 10 minutes of charging gives you around five hours of playback, with a full recharge taking approximately two hours. Although they lack ANC and adjustable EQ, these headphones still have plenty of extra features for Apple users, and those shortcomings are much easier to forgive at almost 66% off. For $69, the Beats Solo 4 headphones are a compact and well-equipped option for casual listening, with long battery life and that classic Beats aesthetic.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump is posthumously pardoning baseball legend Pete Rose, two years after his death.

“I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND,” Trump, 80, posted via Truth Social on Thursday, November 19.

The former professional player, whose career spanned more than two decades, died of heart disease at age 83 at his Las Vegas home in September 2024. Prior to his death, Rose pleaded guilty in 1990 to two felony counts of filing false federal tax income returns, for which he served five months in prison.

Rose, the all-time hits leader in Major League Baseball history, became a superstar with the Reds from 1963 to 1978. He would later return to the Reds in 1984 and play the final three seasons of his professional career with the franchise, when he also acted as a player-manager for the team until 1989.

According to recent reports, in August 1989, during his final year as Reds’ manager, Rose was permanently banned from baseball after allegations that he gambled on games during his playing career. The accusations suggested Rose placed wagers on games involving his own team.

Industry observers note that rose was subsequently banned from being eligible for the Major League Baseball Hall of Fame, despite being one of the league’s most decorated and beloved players in history. The exclusion of Rose has been a point of contention in the baseball community for decades.

In May 2025, Major League Baseball commissioner, Rob Manfred, reinstated Rose to the MLB, which opened the door for him to be posthumously inducted into the Hall of Fame.

After years of public denial, Rose admitted the allegations against him were true in 2004, but he continued to fight for his reinstatement when he was still alive.

Industry observers note that “For me, the thrill wasn’t about the odds. I got involved because I was rooting for my teams — no, believing in my teams. I bet the Reds to win every time. I bet the Phillies to win even though they were huge underdogs and on a losing streak,” he wrote via his 2004 memoir, My Prison Without Bars. “It wasn’t the smart way to bet. But it was my gut feeling … and I always bet with my gut. I never — ever — bet against my teams. If I had, I’d be doubting everything I believed in. And, hell, to my way of thinking, we were going to win every night. You can’t be a competitor and think otherwise.”.

Despite his controversial past that eventually led to him being banned from baseball, Rose was remembered by the League after news of his death broke in 2024.

In a recent development, “Major League Baseball extends its deepest condolences to Pete Rose’s family, his friends across the game, and the fans of his hometown of Cincinnati, Philadelphia, Montreal and beyond who admired his greatness, grit and determination on the field of play,” the official MLB account wrote via X at the time. “May he rest in peace.”.

Industry News: Want To Start Lifting Effectively? GTA 6 Is A Good Teacher
